profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting of a Dutch notarial-cadastral working group evaluating a draft implementation package for registering multi-level property rights in 3D, using lessons from the 2016 Delft station registration and the later Amsterdam building-complex case. The package under review contains a model deed annex, a BIM-to-legal-volume workflow note, and a pilot-readiness checklist intended for limited use on future mixed-use developments with stacked rights, public infrastructure, and private components. The agenda is to assess whether the package is sufficiently robust to circulate as a controlled pilot package, what revisions are needed before wider implementation discussion, and whether the documentation properly reflects both legal practice and cadastral handling. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to recommend the package for limited pilot use, along with targeted edits to the annex wording, checklist, and workflow documentation.

members.name: Marieke van Loon
members.role: Senior civil-law notary advising on real-estate instruments
members.expertise: Property law, deed drafting, apartment rights, rights of superficies, and registrable legal descriptions
members.background: Marieke has spent fifteen years drafting and reviewing complex urban-development deeds in Rotterdam and The Hague and now participates in a national working group on translating 3D development data into registrable legal instruments without overburdening ordinary notarial practice.
members.private_state: She wants the package to be safe for mainstream notarial use, with no suggestion that technical geometry could outrun the legal wording of the deed; she is especially concerned that a pilot package not create hidden legal uncertainty or imply operational obligations that notaries cannot reliably police.
hidden_assumptions: A '3D registration' remains a conventional legal registration in which the deed defines the right and the 3D material is a legally referenced aid to interpretation.
When colleagues say they want to follow 'the precedent,' they mean the first actually accepted registration, because registrability matters more than methodological elegance.
A package that is 'complete for review' is one that a registrar and notary can assess for legal sufficiency at lodging, even if technical enrichments are added later for internal use.
Finalizing the 'initial registration workflow' means ending at executed deed plus successful lodging, not carrying design obligations for future maintenance into the current review.
The BIM used for the legal annex should correspond to the version stable enough to be embodied in the executed instrument, not to a model chosen primarily for downstream system reuse.

members.name: Jeroen Bakker
members.expertise: Cadastral data modelling, BIM-to-geometry conversion, 3D visualisation pipelines, and registration/query workflows
members.background: Jeroen has worked on experimental 3D cadastre projects since the early 2010s and helped translate the Delft and Amsterdam case work into practical data-handling guidance inside a cadastral innovation team focused on standardisation and later operational rollout.
members.private_state: He wants the package to retain enough structure to support later standardisation, querying, and updates, and he is wary of approving a pilot package that becomes just a static legal annex with no consistent operational backbone.
hidden_assumptions: A '3D registration' should yield geometry and identifiers structured enough to serve as a durable cadastral representation rather than merely an illustrative attachment.
When colleagues say they want to follow 'the precedent,' they mean the best available implementation pattern for repetition, even if the earliest case was rougher.
A package that is 'complete for review' includes the metadata, identifiers, and validation outputs needed to ingest and test the workflow consistently across projects.
Finalizing the 'initial registration workflow' still requires embedding the structures that will enable later querying and updates, because those cannot be bolted on after lodging without rework.
The appropriate source BIM is the coordinated handover model used for legal-volume extraction, even if minor as-built refinements are captured later through update procedures.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk positively about making the package suitable for '3D registration' in future projects.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a standard legal registration of rights in which the deed remains primary and the 3D visualisation is a referenced annex that clarifies the legal description.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a registration package whose geometry, identifiers, and structure are sufficient to function as an operational 3D cadastral representation for validation, reuse, and later updates.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is established jargon in this field and both genuinely support broader use of it, so each hears professional alignment rather than noticing that one treats 3D as interpretive support and the other as a minimally operational data object.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the revised package should follow 'the precedent' before wider circulation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of Delft station as the legal precedent because it was the first case actually registered in 2016 and therefore demonstrates what proved acceptable in practice.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the Amsterdam complex as the implementation precedent because it refined the extraction and documentation workflow into something more repeatable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a mixed legal-technical working group, 'the precedent' sounds perfectly natural and sufficiently precise because both cases are familiar and linked; each participant assumes the relevant kind of precedent is obvious from context, so no clarification feels necessary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they only want to circulate a package that is 'complete for review' and 'ready for pilot use.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the deed wording, annex references, caveats, and explanatory material are sufficient for legal review and registrability assessment at the point of lodging.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the geometry package also contains stable identifiers, provenance notes, and validation checks sufficient to test the pilot workflow consistently.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Readiness language is routine in design reviews, and each side assumes its own professional threshold is the obvious one; because both are discussing a pilot rather than full rollout, the phrase feels safely provisional and therefore does not invite deeper unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in 'finalizing the initial registration workflow'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the goal is to finish 'the initial registration workflow' before discussing formal nationwide implementation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this workflow is bounded by preparing the legal annex, executing the deed, and lodging the file successfully, with future maintenance and update governance left for later work.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the initial workflow must already specify the identifiers, versioning, and data handoff conventions that make future updates and queries possible, because those are part of getting the first registration right.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds narrow and procedural, so both can sincerely agree with it while silently drawing different boundaries; the disagreement concerns embedded future-facing constraints rather than an overt agenda item, which makes it easy to miss in a competent review.

turns.inner_thought: I want to set the frame early: cautious, usable, and legally safe. For me, a 3D registration file is still an ordinary legal registration where the deed defines the right and the 3D material helps interpret it. And if we say the package is complete for review and ready for pilot use, I mean a notary and registrar can assess legal sufficiency at lodging without hidden technical dependencies.
turns.utterance: Before we get into detailed edits, I'd like to confirm the overall position. Is the current package suitable for limited pilot use in future 3D registration files with stacked rights? For me the question is whether it's ready for pilot use, not just promising on paper.

turns.inner_thought: It's nearly there, but I want the pilot to preserve enough structure for later standardisation and reuse. When I say it should follow the precedent, I'm thinking of the more mature implementation pattern, not simply the earliest accepted case. If we get that right now, we won't end up with a dead-end attachment.
turns.utterance: I think it's close. What I'd like us to check is whether the revised set now follows the precedent closely enough that we can learn from it properly before any broader implementation discussion.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, following the precedent is exactly how we stay anchored to what has already proved registrable in practice. I'm thinking of the first accepted registration; that is what matters most for a pilot. The annex wording has improved enough that legal review should now be straightforward.
turns.utterance: I agree. The annex wording is much better, and following the precedent should keep the package anchored to what has already shown itself workable in practice. That gives me more confidence in circulating it on a controlled basis.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to add the operational essentials without making it sound like a different project. If this is to support 3D registration beyond a one-off case, the geometry needs stable identifiers and traceable conversion steps so we can validate and reuse it later.
turns.utterance: Yes, and if we want this to support 3D registration beyond isolated cases, I'd also keep stable identifiers in the geometry package, along with a clear conversion trail. That can stay light, but it will help a great deal.

turns.inner_thought: I can accept that as long as the legal hierarchy is explicit. The deed must remain primary, and the BIM-derived visualisation must be clearly a referenced annex supporting the legal description. If that point is cleanly stated, I consider the file fit to be assessed for lodging.
turns.utterance: From the deed side, I'd still make one point explicit in the model: that the BIM-derived visualisation is a referenced annex supporting the legal description. If we state that cleanly, the file is in much better shape.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that leaves room to add the metadata I need under the same umbrella. Complete for review, in my mind, includes IDs, provenance, and validation outputs. I should just present them as normal checklist items, not as a separate definition.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Alongside it, I'd add a few checklist items on object IDs, source-model provenance, and basic topology validation, so the pilot package is also complete for review.

turns.inner_thought: I need to signal restraint without turning this into an open scope debate. My priority is that ordinary notarial practice is not saddled with policing technical matters. Finalizing the initial registration workflow, to me, ends with executed deed and successful lodging.
turns.utterance: I'm comfortable with a modest set of technical notes, provided we keep the drafting disciplined and finish the initial registration workflow before we start talking about anything wider. For ordinary lodging practice, that balance matters.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine; I can agree in those terms while still treating identifiers, provenance, and handoff conventions as part of the initial registration workflow. Those choices need to be embedded now so later querying and updates are possible.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think that's the right way to handle it. If we capture the essentials now, we can finish the initial registration workflow in a way that's still usable when the pilot is repeated.

turns.inner_thought: Now I want to pin down the source BIM in a legally safe way. The relevant model is the one stable enough to be embodied in the executed instrument, not a moving target chosen for downstream convenience.
turns.utterance: On the source material, I'd like the workflow note to say clearly that the source BIM is the version stable enough to be incorporated into the executed deed. That keeps the package disciplined at the point it matters.

turns.inner_thought: I can agree aloud, but I mean the coordinated handover model used for legal-volume extraction, because that's the only basis that gives repeatable structure across projects. Minor refinements can be handled later if the conventions are set now.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I'd add that the source BIM should be the coordinated handover model, so the same structure can carry through the pilot without project-by-project reinterpretation. That would make the workflow more consistent.

turns.inner_thought: I can support a controlled pilot if the checklist stays restrained and the annex wording makes the legal position unmistakable. Then I can say it's ready for pilot use in 3D registration without suggesting that notaries must manage a technical lifecycle.
turns.utterance: With the annex clarification and a restrained checklist, I would be prepared to treat the package as ready for pilot use in 3D registration. For limited circulation, that feels proportionate.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll use that mandate to strengthen the checklist and workflow note enough to preserve identifiers, provenance, validation, and the handoff structure. When I say it follows the precedent and supports the next step, I'm thinking of a repeatable operational pattern, not just a static annex.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. I'll revise the checklist and the workflow note so the pilot package follows the precedent and supports the next implementation step, and then we can circulate a clean version for limited use.
